buyer: African companies paying suppliers in another African currency
finding: A payment from Lagos to Nairobi is still routed through a bank outside Africa and converted into dollars or euros first, adding a conversion, a correspondent fee and days of delay to every intra-African invoice.
number_given: Africa has about 42 currencies; PAPSS is projected to save businesses up to USD 5bn a year in transaction costs if adopted at scale.
source_title: Pan-African Payment and Settlement System
quote: Previously, African companies and their local banks used correspondent banks – often outside of Africa – to settle payments between two African currencies in a third, external currency, usually dollars or Euros.

finding: Every export deal is throttled by a persistent financing gap plus a shrinking list of foreign banks willing to hold correspondent lines for African institutions.
number_given: Trade finance gap put at about US$74bn in 2025; the bank names declining correspondent banking relationships as a direct cause.
source_title: Afreximbank Africa Trade Report shows Africa can turn geopolitical distribution into long-term growth opportunity
quote: Africa’s export performance remains constrained by a persistent trade finance gap, estimated at approximately US$74 billion in 2025. The challenge is exacerbated by limited foreign exchange liquidity and the continued decline in correspondent banking relationships

buyer: Exporters and suppliers selling into African markets
finding: Nearly all intra-African trade runs on open account with almost no credit insurance, so a supplier extending terms to a new foreign buyer is carrying the full default risk on its own balance sheet.
number_given: West Africa's trade finance gap is put at $14bn with bank rejection rates of 21% of applications; globally trade credit insurance underpins about 15% of invoices versus under 5% in Africa.
source_title: Trade Credit Insurance in Africa: New Tinubu x ICISA Whitepaper
publisher: Tinubu with ICISA (International Credit Insurance & Surety Association)
quote: Over 90% of intra-African trade is conducted on open account, and less than 5% is covered by credit insurance.

buyer: African banks and the corporates they lend to
finding: Only about a quarter of African trade passes through a bank at all, so most of a mid-sized firm's cross-border volume runs on open account with no instrument, no guarantee and no bank standing behind it.
number_given: Bank intermediation fell to 23% of African merchandise trade in 2020-2024 from 40% in 2011-19, against roughly 80% globally; AfDB's Anthony Simpasa warns a tighter correspondent risk appetite could push the gap to $86.6bn-$102.6bn by 2027.
source_title: Africa's trade finance gap could widen to $86.6bn as Middle East tensions linger
quote: Banks intermediated an average of just 23 percent of Africa’s merchandise trade between 2020 and 2024, compared to 40 percent in the 2011–19 period.

finding: The financing a $10m-$5bn African firm needs to ship or buy on terms is not there at any price for a large slice of demand, so orders are lost to whoever can self-fund or pay cash.
number_given: $74bn of unmet demand equals 5.4% of Africa's merchandise trade in 2024; 36% of banks cite FX liquidity as the top constraint and banks now intermediate only 23% of trade versus 40% pre-2020.
source_title: AM2026: AfDB 2025 Trade Finance Report Highlights Resilience of African Financial Institutions After Covid-19
quote: The unmet demand for trade finance in Africa ranged from $74 billion to $92 billion in 2024.

finding: The paperwork and checkpoint costs, not tariffs, are what make intra-African trade expensive: duplicate documents, inconsistent standards and unofficial fees, with a reporting mechanism most firms never use.
number_given: AfCFTA is projected to lift intra-African trade by more than 50% if NTBs are cut; the reviews found national NTB committees under-resourced or inactive and resolution speed varying widely.
source_title: Lessons from AfCFTA Readiness Reviews: Lesson #2: Tackling Non-Tariff Barriers
publisher: Trade Policy Training Centre in Africa (trapca), AfDB/ACBF-funded AfCFTA Readiness Reviews
quote: These obstacles, which include excessive paperwork, protracted clearance processes, inconsistent standards, and hidden fees, often represent the real cost of doing business in Africa.

finding: The Atlantic is the expensive part: costly shipping, fragmented regulation on both sides and thin trade finance make a first Africa-Caribbean transaction hard to price and hard to close.
number_given: Trade and compliance specialist Eliot Kelly, on the record: the biggest barrier is not geography or history but the cost and complexity of doing business across the Atlantic; Afreximbank has raised CARICOM financing to $5bn.
source_title: Africa-Caribbean trade faces major hurdles
quote: Yet turning those connections into profitable business remains difficult, with costly shipping, fragmented regulations and limited trade finance standing in the way.

finding: Currency moves on dollar-denominated input and funding costs wipe out operating profit for a large manufacturer, leaving it technically insolvent on net assets even while sales grow.
number_given: Net loss N164.6bn for 2024; net finance cost N389.5bn; net assets negative N92.3bn; total borrowings up 62% to N653.7bn.
source_title: Nestle posts N164.6bn net loss for 2024, on FX losses, interest rate
quote: Its net FX losses also surged to N290.7 billion, however, only N57.6 billion of that sum was realised.

buyer: Nigeria Customs Service / importers at Tin Can Island, Lagos
finding: Even where customs clears a shipment in three days, a large minority of consignments sit in the port beyond ten days, and the tail runs to months, because inspections are physical and uncoordinated.
number_given: Longest case 122 days; only 1% of consignments scanned (44 minutes average) versus 99% physically examined (nearly five days); Customs puts the annual saving from reform at about N3trn in demurrage and trade costs.
source_title: Customs says port reforms could cut cargo delays 40%, save N3trn annually
quote: About 98.7% of shipments are cleared in an average of three days and 14 hours, yet 43% of consignments remain in the port for more than 10 days before final exit.

buyer: NAFDAC and other inspection agencies / importers of food, drugs and cosmetics
finding: Importing a regulated product means inspection and certification by agencies that cannot process the volume, so clearance slips by weeks and the importer carries the demurrage.
number_given: The same guide records complaints from healthcare and processed-food companies about exorbitant NAFDAC registration fees and very long processing timelines, flagged as technical barriers to trade.
source_title: Nigeria - Trade Barriers
publisher: U.S. International Trade Administration (Country Commercial Guide: Nigeria)
quote: Most goods destined for Nigeria, especially in the food, drug, and cosmetics, require inspection or certification from authorities or appointed third-party contractors.

buyer: Federal Government procurement / foreign suppliers and investors
finding: Local content rules and a mandatory local incorporation requirement mean a foreign counterparty cannot simply contract with a Nigerian firm - the structure has to be rebuilt before any deal can be signed.
number_given: Section 78 of CAMA obliges a foreign company to incorporate a separate Nigerian entity before doing business; local content now extends beyond oil and gas into ICT and advertising.
source_title: Nigeria - Trade Barriers
publisher: U.S. International Trade Administration (Country Commercial Guide: Nigeria)
quote: An Executive Order from 2017 mandates that at least 40% of government procurement spending on specific categories, such as pharmaceuticals, uniforms, and IT products, be directed toward locally made goods.

buyer: Transnet / Durban Container Terminal Pier 2 (Durban Gateway Terminal)
finding: At the terminal handling 46% of South Africa's containers, vessels wait days at anchor and shipping lines add congestion surcharges, so exporters cannot quote a reliable delivery date to an overseas buyer.
number_given: Average vessel wait of 99 hours through July 2026; some containers delayed up to three weeks with congestion surcharges added; terminal handles about 46% of national container traffic.
source_title: Durban Gateway Terminal: the push to end persistent cargo delays
quote: TNPA reported in September that DCT Pier 2 had recorded an average vessel wait of 99 hours through July 2026.

buyer: Importers and exporters using regional ports
finding: Cargo sits in African ports for roughly three weeks, so working capital is tied up in containers and delivery dates promised to a foreign buyer cannot be held.
number_given: Cargo from port to a landlocked country spends 75% of its time at the port rather than on the road; under a week in large Asian, European and Latin American ports.
source_title: Why does cargo sit so long in African ports? Not just poor infrastructure... poor incentives
publisher: World Bank (Africa Can End Poverty blog)
quote: Cargo spends nearly three weeks on average in Sub-Saharan African ports, compared to under a week in large ports in Asia, Europe and Latin America.

buyer: Traders, freight forwarders and drivers surveyed across 8 ECOWAS countries
finding: Traders are still stopped for certificates of origin and duplicate sanitary certificates that regional rules abolished decades ago, each one costing most of a working day and a cash fee at the border.
number_given: COO: 15 hours and $41.74 on average; duplicate phytosanitary certificates nearly 13 hours and $68.28; duplicate zoosanitary certificates just under 19 hours and $57.76 - survey of 290 traders across 20 border points.
source_title: Hub survey quantifies time and cost spent on West African trade barriers
publisher: tralac / USAID West Africa Trade and Investment Hub
quote: Traders said they were required to obtain a COO more than half of the time, which took them an average of 15 hours and cost an average $41.74.

buyer: Public Procurement Regulatory Authority / Ministry of Finance
finding: Tenders and whole sectors are reserved or scored in favour of citizen-owned firms, so foreign bidders must find a local partner before they can compete at all.
number_given: Under the 2021 Public Procurement Act the Minister of Finance sets preference margins on ownership, location, labour source and subcontracting; investors complain of 'the perception that investment requires a local partner who may add limited value'.
publisher: U.S. Department of State (2026 Investment Climate Statements)
quote: Some sectors and public contracts are reserved or preferred for citizen-owned firms, so foreign investors often partner with local companies to access tenders and preference schemes.

buyer: Afreximbank / Pan-African Payment and Settlement System (PAPSS)
finding: Currency inconvertibility traps investor capital inside African jurisdictions, so returns cannot be repatriated even when the project itself works.
number_given: Over $2bn is currently trapped in African countries where airlines operate, unable to repatriate; reliance on hard currency for intra-African settlement drains an estimated $5bn a year in fees, delays and opportunity costs.
publisher: Pan-African Payment and Settlement System (PAPSS) / Afreximbank
quote: Corporations, airlines, reinsurance firms, and multinationals operating across Africa still faced a persistent hurdle: trapped capital, arising from limited currency convertibility and overreliance on hard currencies.

buyer: AfCFTA Secretariat / national focal points / customs authorities
finding: The continental mechanism for clearing non-tariff barriers stalls on unresponsive, under-resourced national focal points, so reported barriers stay open and traders keep paying for them.
number_given: The AfCFTA NTB Online Mechanism is the official channel for customs delays, ad hoc fees and documentary barriers; at the first REC coordination meeting (Lomé, 18 March 2025) the Secretariat recorded weak responsiveness from designated focal points as a core blocker.
quote: They also shared regional updates, best practices, and outlined challenges, including resource constraints and the need for improved responsiveness from designated focal points.

buyer: Autorité de Régulation de la Commande Publique (ARCOP) / Ministry of Finance and Budget
finding: Procurement is open on paper but opaque in practice, with contracts awarded outside tender and sole-sourcing justified by urgency.
number_given: The report notes sole-source awards made citing 'the high technical capacity of a firm or a declared emergency', and that many firms still cite corruption as an obstacle to transparent award decisions.
publisher: U.S. Department of State (2026 Investment Climate Statement: Côte d'Ivoire, PDF)
quote: While the public procurement process is open by law, in practice it is opaque, and government contracts are occasionally awarded outside of public tenders.

buyer: Ministry of Finance / Ghana Investment Promotion Authority (GIPA)
finding: Arrears owed to local and international companies are large enough to be cited as a drag on investor confidence, alongside debt and revenue shortfalls.
number_given: The same report lists government steps that hurt confidence, including 'undermine contract sanctity by not paying its arrears' and local content rules imposed 'without allowing sufficient time to transition'.
publisher: U.S. Department of State (2026 Investment Climate Statements)
quote: While Ghana’s economy has recovered from the 2022 financial crisis, with GDP growth rebounding significantly from 2.9 percent in 2023 to 6 percent in 2025, concerns persist around high public debt levels, arrears owed to local and international companies, and structural revenue shortfalls.

buyer: Ministry of Lands / county governments / implementing agencies
finding: Land ownership and registration records are unreliable enough that title disputes stall nationally significant projects.
number_given: Only 30,016 mortgages recorded nationwide as of 2024 in a country of about 53 million people; the report also notes property rights are weakly enforced.
publisher: U.S. Department of State (2026 Investment Climate Statements)
quote: The legal infrastructure around land ownership and registration has changed in recent years, and land issues delayed several major infrastructure projects.

buyer: National Treasury / Controller of Budget / state corporations
finding: Verified bills owed to contractors and suppliers keep growing, so firms that win public contracts cannot be paid on schedule and discount the deal accordingly.
number_given: Sh511.75bn total pending bills, up 5.1% year-on-year; contractors and development projects alone hold Sh259.7bn (51%) and state corporations Sh421.63bn (82%).
publisher: The Eastleigh Voice (reporting the Controller of Budget's Budget Implementation Review Report)
quote: Margaret Nyakang’o’s report puts the total pending bills by the national government at Sh511.75 billion as of March 31, 2025, up from Sh486.81 billion recorded at the same time last year.

buyer: Ministry of Justice / Office of the Attorney-General / Namibia Investment Promotion and Development Board
finding: Foreign arbitral awards cannot be enforced in Namibia, so any deal that sours has no reliable neutral exit for the investor.
number_given: Only holders of a Certificate of Status Investment can opt for international arbitration and be compensated in foreign currency; work-permit and visa renewals are also reported as slow.
publisher: U.S. Department of State (2026 Investment Climate Statements)
quote: Namibia is also not a party to the Convention on the Recognition and Enforcement of Foreign Arbitral Awards (New York Convention).

buyer: Nigerian Ports Authority / Nigeria Customs Service
finding: Cargo dwell times at the main Lagos ports remain above three weeks because examinations are still manual, adding a hidden cost to every import-dependent investment.
number_given: Over 20 days dwell versus Lekki Deep Seaport, which handled $9.6bn of trade in 2025 at 50 percent capacity; the report calls port inefficiency a 'hidden tax' on investment.
publisher: U.S. Department of State (2026 Investment Climate Statements)
quote: traditional ports in Apapa and Tin Can still suffer from cargo dwell times exceeding 20 days due to manual examinations.

buyer: Rwanda Revenue Authority / Rwanda Development Board
finding: Statutory VAT refunds to foreign investors run months or years late because they wait behind open audits, and retroactive fines follow.
number_given: 30-day statutory refund becomes months-to-years in practice; investors also cite punitive retroactive fines from indefinite audits.
publisher: U.S. Department of State (2026 Investment Climate Statements)
quote: By law, foreign firms should receive value-added tax (VAT) rebates within 30 days of receipt by the Rwanda Revenue Authority (RRA); however, firms complained the process for reimbursement can take months and occasionally years.

buyer: Ministry of Justice / courts / Agence de Régulation des Marchés Publics (ARMP)
finding: Foreign investors do not trust local courts to hear cases involving the state and route disputes offshore, which leaves government contracts contested in forums it does not control.
number_given: Reported complaints also include excessive and inconsistently applied tax and customs penalties, a lack of commercial arbitration mechanisms, and opaque decision-making for public contracts.
publisher: U.S. Department of State (2026 Investment Climate Statements)
quote: Some foreign investors, however, report discriminatory treatment by local courts and usually seek arbitration proceedings in international court when possible.

buyer: Prime Minister's Office / Ministry of Investment, Industry and Trade
finding: Approvals sit across ministries that do not coordinate, and negotiations with government to start a project drag on without a closing date.
number_given: Investors also report the Tanzania Revenue Authority does not recognise incentives granted under signed framework agreements, so negotiated terms do not survive implementation.
publisher: U.S. Department of State (2026 Investment Climate Statements)
quote: The government’s bureaucracy and slow coordination between ministries and offices result in delays that have halted investments for years.

buyer: Tanzania Investment and Special Economic Zones Authority (TISEZA) / Ministry of Lands
finding: Foreign investors cannot own land at all; they must obtain a specific investment-purpose approval before any project site can be secured.
number_given: Approval must come from the Tanzania Investment and Special Economic Zones Authority (TISEZA); even with TISEZA's land bank, the report states restrictions on foreign ownership 'may significantly delay investments'.
publisher: U.S. Department of State (2026 Investment Climate Statements)
quote: Foreigners are also prohibited from owning land in Tanzania, with the exception of specific investment purposes

buyer: Ministry of Finance and National Planning / Zambia Revenue Authority
finding: Government pays vendors and VAT refunds late as a budgeting habit, which works as an unlegislated tax on the companies it has contracted.
number_given: Businesses also cite difficulty obtaining work permits for expatriate staff and non-transparent government tenders; public procurement of services under ZMW 3 million (~$160,000) is closed to foreign participation.
publisher: U.S. Department of State (2026 Investment Climate Statements)
quote: Companies have also reported that, due to ongoing fiscal constraints, the government’s payments to vendors and VAT refunds to companies are often significantly delayed, presenting an additional de facto private sector tax.

finding: CARICOM's own trade machinery is clogged with non-compliance and ad hoc exemptions: the Secretariat processed 192 Common External Tariff suspension requests and 66 safeguard invocations in a single year, and the Secretary-General says removing 'non-compliance' from the agenda is still an imperative.
number_given: In the same remarks the Secretary-General said the Region has an imperative to address the impediments to trade and remove longstanding issues of non-compliance from the agenda. Separately, CARICOM's Annual Report 2024 records that the Secretary-General processed 192 requests for suspension of the CET and 66 requests for invocation of the Safeguard Mechanism in one year, from 12 member states.
publisher: CARICOM Secretariat (Secretary-General Dr Carla Barnett, 60th COTED)
quote: We need to promote regional production and expand intra-regional trade by updating policies and practices to support entrepreneurship and make trade and business development easier.

finding: Caribbean central bank governors say the region cannot keep depending on US correspondent banks, and the replacement - a CARICOM-wide local-currency settlement system linked to Africa's PAPSS - is still only a pilot.
number_given: CAPSS pilot covers Barbados, The Bahamas and ECCB member states plus one further country; linking to Africa is explicitly 'phase two', only after the intra-CARICOM pilot completes.
publisher: Jamaica Gleaner (quoting ECCB Governor Timothy Antoine, on the record)
quote: We cannot continue to rely on correspondent banks, particularly from the US

finding: Caribbean exports are taxed punitively in African markets - rum, the region's flagship branded export, faces an 88 percent tariff - which removes the reciprocal commercial case for a deal.
number_given: Bilateral exports between the two regions have never surpassed 6 percent; African exports to the Caribbean have been close to 0.1 percent since 2020. Interregional trade is US$729 million against a potential US$2.1 billion within five years.
publisher: Afreximbank (op-ed by ITC Executive Director Pamela Coke-Hamilton and Afreximbank President Benedict Oramah)
quote: Caribbean rum exporters currently face an 88% tariff when selling to African markets

finding: Correspondent banks have withdrawn from Caribbean jurisdictions, raising the cost of every international transaction and cutting firms off from the payment system entirely.
number_given: Paper quantifies de-risking across CARICOM and finds trade financing and remittances were the two most affected areas; notes Bank of America withdrew correspondent operations from Belize Bank and Atlantic Bank in 2015 and Barclays severed ties with Jamaica.
publisher: Central Bank of Trinidad and Tobago (working paper, April 2020)
quote: In the Caribbean the increased global scrutiny of activities of financial firms resulted in correspondent banks withdrawing their services from several of the islands, increasing costs of conducting international transactions

finding: Cross-border payment rails are the structural blocker: Caribbean payments still run through US correspondent banks, and the region has no local-currency settlement with Africa, so every deal carries an extra hop, extra cost and extra counterparty risk.
number_given: Note states that over the medium term 'payment systems to settle non-USD transactions and expanded trade finance' are still needed; current routing through the US is described as reinforcing dependence on incumbent supply chains.
publisher: World Bank (Trade and Connectivity in the Caribbean, Policy Note, July 2026)
quote: Payment systems routed through the U.S. and lack of trade finance further reinforce path dependency on existing arrangements.

finding: Customs and border clearance is slow and expensive: an import shipment takes two weeks to clear and clearance costs alone absorb more than a third of the goods' value.
number_given: Average across World Bank Enterprise Surveys in Antigua and Barbuda (2025), Barbados (2023), Jamaica (2024), St. Lucia (2025), Suriname (2025) and Trinidad and Tobago (2025). 63 percent of firms use imported inputs, averaging 38 percent of total inputs.
publisher: World Bank (Trade and Connectivity in the Caribbean, Policy Note, July 2026)
quote: it takes on average 14 days for an import shipment to clear customs and border agencies, and the costs associated amount to 36 percent of the value of the goods

finding: De-risking has left legitimate Caribbean businesses and new ventures without banking access at all - not because of wrongdoing but because compliance cost exceeds correspondent bank profit.
number_given: Barbados central bank notes terminations are driven by compliance cost under Basel, FATCA and Global Forum rules rather than any wrongdoing by Caribbean businesses; a CARICOM Central Bank Governors Technical Work Group was assembled to assess regional impact.
quote: The consequence of this is that many businesses and individuals have been cut off from their money and new businesses are finding it difficult to establish operations.

finding: Logistics, not demand, is what kills Africa-Caribbean trade: the majority of unrealized trade potential is lost to transport and logistics failure, and there is no direct sea or air link.
number_given: The regions are 1,600 miles apart yet lack direct transport links; both rank among the lowest in the world on World Bank logistics performance. Ocean freight between West African and Caribbean ports typically routes via Europe or North America.
publisher: Afreximbank (op-ed by ITC Executive Director Pamela Coke-Hamilton and Afreximbank President Benedict Oramah)
quote: ITC data show that 57% of unrealized trade potential stems from logistical challenges.

finding: Moving goods into and out of the Caribbean costs multiples of the global norm, which makes any African-origin shipment uncompetitive before it lands.
number_given: Caribbean countries spend roughly 12-21 percent of the value of imported goods on international transport and insurance versus a global average of about 7.5 percent; Suriname sits around three times the world average.
publisher: World Bank (Trade and Connectivity in the Caribbean, Policy Note, July 2026)
quote: Caribbean transport costs are among the highest globally, and they are even more acute for food

finding: Not all CARICOM states have even joined Afreximbank's Partnership Agreement, which caps the financing envelope available for cross-border projects and leaves some governments outside the only Africa-facing trade finance institution.
number_given: The communique 'APPLAUD[s] the 13 countries that have signed onto Afreximbank's Partnership Agreement' and urges the rest to formalise - meaning some CARICOM members still have no access to the Bank's project and trade facilities.
publisher: Afreximbank / Government of Grenada (Fourth AfriCaribbean Trade and Investment Forum Communique, ACTIF2025)
quote: urge remaining countries to formalize participation in order to fully benefit from tailored financing, facilitation and advisory services

finding: Sanitary and phytosanitary approval is the hidden gate on any new African food or agricultural supplier: no risk assessment exists, none is published, and getting one can take years.
number_given: The note also finds there is no comprehensive publicly available information on individual CARICOM countries' SPS import requirements or existing risk assessments by product-origin pair, so a supplier cannot even check the requirement.
publisher: World Bank (Trade and Connectivity in the Caribbean, Policy Note, July 2026)
quote: If a risk assessment has not been conducted by the importing country on the particular product-origin (e.g., limes from Mexico), such an analysis is required, and it may take weeks or years to be prepared.

finding: Signature is not ratification: of 15 CARICOM member states, 12 acceded but only nine completed ratification, and the region's financing ceiling doubles only when all 15 join - so the money is gated on domestic parliamentary process.
number_given: US$1.5 billion financing limit approved for the region, set to double to US$3 billion once all CARICOM member states join; the 2026 announcement raised the global cap to US$5 billion with over US$750 million already disbursed.
quote: 12 of the 15 CARICOM member states have now acceded to the Partnership Agreement, with nine of them concluding its ratification.

finding: Tariff and non-tariff barriers close the Caribbean market to non-traditional suppliers, including African ones, even where shipping exists.
number_given: Average MFN tariff around 13.2 percent in CARICOM; NTMs documented across nine Caribbean countries using the UNCTAD NTM database.
publisher: World Bank (Trade and Connectivity in the Caribbean, Policy Note, July 2026)
quote: Policy and regulatory frictions, including elevated Most Favored Nation (MFN) tariffs, averaging around 13.2 percent in CARICOM, and complex non-tariff measures (NTMs) and standards, further impede direct sourcing from alternative suppliers.

finding: The Africa-Caribbean Free Trade Arrangement that would de-risk cross-border deals is, as of the 2025 Heads-level communique, only 'endorsed' for establishment - while Afreximbank itself names inadequate transport, scarce trade and project finance, and regulatory misalignment as the persistent barriers.
number_given: The communique only 'WELCOME[s] the endorsement for the establishment and operationalization of an Africa-Caribbean Free Trade Arrangement' and 'UNDERTAKE[s] to support, and fast-track' air and maritime links - i.e. neither instrument exists yet.
publisher: Afreximbank / Government of Grenada (Fourth AfriCaribbean Trade and Investment Forum Communique, ACTIF2025)
quote: the persistent structural barriers to AfriCaribbean integration, including inadequate transportation and connectivity, limited access to trade and project finance, and regulatory misalignment

finding: Trinidad and Tobago, the region's industrial exporter, runs a structural foreign exchange shortage - demand for USD permanently exceeds supply, forcing central bank intervention.
number_given: Presidential presentation describes a 'structural imbalance' in the FX market; the Bank's own monetary policy report records a net sales gap of US$1,274.1 million over January-October 2025 with US$1,087.7 million of central bank intervention to support the market.
publisher: Central Bank of Trinidad and Tobago (Governor Larry Howai, presentation 4 September 2025)
quote: Constraints remain in the domestic foreign exchange market as demand continues to outstrip supply.

finding: Digital skills and telecoms capacity gaps are explicitly named as hampering regional development, which is why so much of this trade cannot be done online yet.
source_title: Fourth AfriCaribbean Trade and Investment Forum Communique
quote: digital skills shortages and capacity gaps in telecommunications and digital sectors that are hampering regional development

finding: Only 13 countries have signed Afreximbank's partnership agreement; the rest have no access to the tailored financing and advisory that makes a cross-regional deal bankable.
number_given: 13 countries signed (source, July 2025)
source_title: Fourth AfriCaribbean Trade and Investment Forum Communique
quote: urge remaining countries to formalize participation in order to fully benefit from tailored financing, facilitation and advisory services

buyer: Heads of State via Afreximbank forum
finding: The Africa-Caribbean Free Trade Arrangement is still at the endorsement stage: its own stated job is to eliminate trade barriers and unlock mutual market access, which means neither exists yet.
source_title: Fourth AfriCaribbean Trade and Investment Forum Communique
quote: to eliminate trade barriers, enhance regulatory coherence, and unlock mutual market access

finding: The three structural barriers to Africa-Caribbean trade are named and unchanged: transport and connectivity, access to trade and project finance, and regulatory misalignment.
source_title: Fourth AfriCaribbean Trade and Investment Forum Communique
quote: inadequate transportation and connectivity, limited access to trade and project finance, and regulatory misalignment

buyer: African Union Commission and CARICOM Secretariat
finding: There is still no direct air or maritime link between Africa and the Caribbean, so every deal needs a transhipment through Europe or North America.
source_title: Fourth AfriCaribbean Trade and Investment Forum Communique
quote: to establish direct air and maritime links between Africa and the Caribbean

sector: AI / Arabic language models and speech
finding: iFlytek signed a three-year research agreement with Egypt's ICT ministry to build Arabic speech recognition, synthesis and Chinese-Arabic translation inside a government AI centre.
number_given: Six milestones over three years; iFlytek to supply Arabic editions of its commercial products and train Egyptian researchers; no contract value disclosed.
source_title: A.I. connects the Silk Road: iFLYTEK signs Arabic-Chinese language translation research agreement with Egyptian Ministry of Communications and Information Technology
quote: The EMCIT's Artificial Intelligence and High-Performance Computing Applications Center and iFLYTEK will develop research projects in Arabic speech recognition, speech synthesis, and Chinese Arabic translation.

finding: Alibaba signed three MoUs with Ethiopia's government to stand up an eWTP hub for cross-border trade, logistics and SME training, its second such hub in Africa.
number_given: Three MoUs signed in Addis Ababa with PM Abiy Ahmed and Jack Ma present; China Commodities City International is the build partner; Alibaba Business School runs training; no investment figure disclosed.
source_title: The Government of Ethiopia and Alibaba Group Sign Agreements to Establish eWTP Ethiopia Hub
quote: The eWTP (electronic world trade platform) Hub is intended to enable cross-border trade, provide smart logistics and fulfillment services, assist Ethiopian small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) to reach China and other markets, and provide talent training.

finding: ZTE supplied and installed Ethiopia's entire national telecom network under a $1.5 billion China Development Bank-backed supplier credit to the state operator.
number_given: $1.5bn CDB export seller's credit at LIBOR+150bps over 10 years, on-lent as a $1.5bn supplier credit with 16.75-year maturity and 3.25-year grace; later rescheduled. Mobile subscribers rose from under 1.2m (2007) to ~17.5m (2012).
source_title: ZTE provides $1.53 billion, CDB-backed supplier's credit for Phases 1-3 of National Telecommunications Network
quote: In this particular case, China Development Bank provided a $1.5 billion export seller's credit to ZTE, and ZTE then used the proceeds of the export seller's credit to lend to the Government of Ethiopia.

finding: Huawei built Nairobi's and Mombasa's Safe City surveillance and command platform with Safaricom, sold to Kenya's National Police Service as a national security strategy.
number_given: No contract value disclosed. Phase one covered Nairobi and Mombasa; Huawei claims a 46% crime drop in covered areas (Kenya Police annual report, 2014-2015). Ecosystem partners listed as Safaricom and Tyco (integrators), Hexagon, Milestone, SAP.
source_title: Huawei Hosts Safe City Summit in Africa to Showcase Industry Best Practices
quote: Additionally, Safaricom, the largest comprehensive telecommunications service provider of Kenya, shared its cooperation with Huawei in the development of the Kenya Safe City project.

finding: Opera incubated OPay in Lagos, raised $50 million from Chinese investors and scaled to 40,000 agents handling over $5 million a day, becoming Nigeria's largest mobile transaction provider.
number_given: $50m round led by IDG Capital, Sequoia China, Source Code Capital, Meituan-Dianping, GSR Ventures and Opera; 40,000+ agents and >$5m daily volume within a year of the August 2018 launch.
source_title: OPay raises $50 million from investors including IDG Capital, Sequoia China, Source Code Capital and Opera
quote: Within less than a year, by June 2019, OPay had more than 40,000 active agents and saw daily transaction volumes in excess of $5 million, propelling the company to become the largest mobile transaction provider in the country.

finding: Transsion's Tecno unit led a $40 million round into PalmPay and pre-installed its wallet on 20 million Tecno, Infinix and Itel phones, buying distribution at the device level.
number_given: $40m seed via Transsion's Tecno subsidiary with NetEase and MediaTek; 20 million pre-installed apps in 2020; Central Bank of Nigeria mobile money licence granted July 2019; 100,000 users and 1m transactions in pilot.
source_title: PalmPay launches in Nigeria on $40M round led by China’s Transsion
quote: As part of the investment, PalmPay enters a strategic partnership with mobile brands Tecno, Infinix and Itel that includes pre-installation of the startup’s app on 20 million phones in 2020.

finding: African governments have spent over $2 billion on Chinese facial recognition and plate-tracking systems, typically bundled into soft loans that name the hardware and command-centre vendors.
number_given: More than $2bn spent across 11 countries; Nigeria alone over $470m, the continent's largest smart-city surveillance buyer; package financing via Chinese soft loans.
source_title: Africa’s rising spending on Chinese surveillance tech
quote: For example, a loan of $250 million from China Eximbank might be tied to the purchase of surveillance cameras from Hikvision and a command and control center built and serviced by Huawei or ZTE.

finding: Huawei opened public cloud regions in Johannesburg and Cape Town to sell cloud and AI infrastructure across southern Africa in direct competition with AWS and Microsoft.
number_given: Two data centres, Johannesburg first then Cape Town, from March 2019; services sold to South Africa and neighbouring countries; capex not disclosed.
source_title: Huawei to build data centers in South Africa
quote: China’s Huawei will build two data centers in South Africa from March, it said, as part of plans to expand cloud services across Africa.

finding: Huawei supplied Uganda Police's $126 million CCTV network, which the force bought while cash-strapped and which opposition figures say is used to track opponents.
number_given: $126 million CCTV system; Uganda Police is the buyer and operator, with Chinese financing and Huawei as supplier.
source_title: Uganda's cash-strapped cops spend $126 million on CCTV from Huawei
quote: Police say the new $126 million closed-circuit television camera (CCTV) system, supplied by Chinese telecommunications giant Huawei Technologies Co Ltd, will slash spiraling violent crime.

finding: Transsion, which ships about half of Africa's smartphones, is now selling TankVolt electric bikes into five African markets and chasing government fleet contracts.
number_given: 9.3 million smartphones shipped to Africa in 2024 (~50% share); TankVolt bikes built in Shenzhen retail about $1,500; battery-as-a-service in Tanzania, Uganda next; targeting government contracts and private fleets.
source_title: Transsion wheels into Africa’s EV market with same playbook that conquered mobile phones
quote: The Chinese company, which controls about half of Africa’s smartphone market, entered the continent’s electric vehicle race by introducing its TankVolt e-bikes in Uganda in 2023.

finding: Huawei delivered Zambia's first 'smart village' with RuralStar base stations, solar micro-grids and school devices, and is pushing DeepSeek models into Zambian public services with the Ministry of Technology and Science.
number_given: Site delivered in 30 days in July 2024; equipment includes micro solar plants, RuralStar base station, IdeaHub devices and electronic blackboards for schools and clinics; no value disclosed.
source_title: Ministry of Technology and Science of Zambia and Huawei Jointly Launch the Global Smart Village Showcase
quote: The extensive use of the DeepSeek model signifies not just a technological advancement, but also a fundamental shift in production dynamics.

finding: CloudWalk signed a framework agreement with Zimbabwe's government to build a national facial recognition database, described at the time as China's first AI push into Africa under the Belt and Road.
number_given: Value not disclosed. CloudWalk, then a $75m-funded startup behind China's 'Police Cloud', supplied the national database; deal signed during a Zimbabwean delegation visit to China.
source_title: Zimbabwe govt selects CloudWalk for mass facial recognition project
quote: Under the agreement, CloudWalk will help the country set up a national facial recognition database, as part of what it described as a mass facial recognition project.

buyer: Egyptian and MEA e-commerce merchants using their own carrier agreements
finding: Fincart bundles multi-carrier shipping with remittance handling and working-capital advances for merchants who cannot get bank credit against their receivables.
number_given: $2.8m seed co-led by Launch Africa Ventures and Antler with Yango Ventures, Five35, Bluestream, Hi2 Global and Kalahari; monetises logistics margin plus credit; no take-rate disclosed.
source_title: Egypt’s Fincart Raises $2.8 Million Seed Round to Expand AI Logistics Platform
quote: Fincart provides an AI-driven platform that helps online merchants simplify shipping, logistics, and remittance operations.

buyer: African banks and fintechs that need card and omni-channel processing without building it
finding: enza gives banks one integration to a modern processing stack instead of legacy switch vendors, and keeps the bank owning its merchants and data.
number_given: $6m seed+ led by 4DX Ventures with BII, Quona and Algebra following on; $12.75m raised across two rounds; pricing not public, sold as per-transaction processing to institutions.
source_title: Egypt’s enza raises $6m seed+ round to expand payments infrastructure across Africa
quote: Banks connect through a single integration to enza’s platform while keeping control of their merchants and data.

buyer: Accra-based SME importers shipping from China, UK, US, Turkey and Dubai
finding: Swiftway takes over customs clearance, haulage and broker paperwork end to end for SME importers whom big forwarders price out and informal brokers rip off.
number_given: Bootstrapped, closing a $100k pre-seed; earns a service fee per shipment covering forwarding margin, customs clearance fees and haulage coordination, with volume agreements for enterprise clients; no Caribbean lane.
source_title: Ghana’s Swiftway is a digital freight forwarding platform built for African businesses
quote: Ghanaian startup Swiftway is a digital freight forwarding platform built for African businesses, handling the full process of air and sea freight, customs clearance, and haulage

buyer: Caribbean remittance senders and mobile wallet customers in Barbados
finding: Zeepay's Barbados subsidiary was suspended by the Central Bank and then wound itself up, showing that a licensed Caribbean beachhead can be lost to supervisory concerns about governance and capital.
number_given: Zeepay founded 2015 and one of Africa's larger cross-border mobile money players; Barbados entity had physical branch costs and no disclosed take-rate; expansion capital not public.
source_title: Zeemoney shuts shop after Central Bank suspension order
quote: Zeemoney (Barbados) Limited, which had four locations across the island, was first forced to pause its business after the Central Bank suspended its licence from May 5 until June 4.

buyer: Guyanese MSMEs importing less-than-container-load goods from the US and other markets
finding: PAS Cargo is the Caribbean-side mirror of the African freight startups: consolidation, brokerage and warehousing for small importers, only now going digital with IDB Lab money.
number_given: Undisclosed IDB Lab financing plus working capital; earns freight consolidation and brokerage fees; import lanes are US-centric with no Africa corridor in scope.
source_title: IDB Lab Supports PAS Cargo to Expand Digital Logistics Services for Small Businesses Across Guyana
quote: PAS Cargo Guyana is a Guyanese logistics and freight forwarding company specializing in the fulfillment of Less than Container Load imports into Guyana and serving primarily MSMEs.

buyer: Caribbean and West African smallholder cooperatives, manufacturers and exporters
finding: Knova and Farm FWD are building the first Caribbean-to-West-Africa trade stack, where customs declarations and compliance certificates are the actual barrier to export.
number_given: No funding figure disclosed; revenue from compliance tooling and embedded trade finance; live link is Jamaica-Ghana only, aligned with the Africa-Caribbean Corridor Council chaired from The Bahamas.
source_title: Jamaica to Ghana: Knova and Farm FWD Connect Farmers to Global Markets
quote: even verified, well-run farms and manufacturers routinely lose market access to paperwork, including customs declarations, compliance certificates

buyer: African and Caribbean diaspora sending remittances, plus traders paying across South-South corridors
finding: WapiPay is the only startup found with a licensed live Africa-to-Caribbean corridor, using JN Money as its Jamaican payout leg for cash collection and bank deposit.
number_given: Funding not disclosed in this report; revenue from FX spread and per-transfer fees; corridors cover Africa, Asia, UK, US and now Jamaica; JN Money operates in 18 countries including Cayman, Antigua, Guyana, Turks and Caicos.
source_title: Kenya’s WapiPay expands into Jamaica to tap $2.5 billion remittance market
quote: The deal will enable WapiPay to facilitate transfers between Africa, Asia, and the Caribbean, targeting both diaspora remittances and trade-linked payments.

buyer: Nigerian SMEs that trade across African borders without in-house legal or logistics staff
finding: Cloud9 automates trade documents, compliance checks and trade finance in one interface because AfCFTA did not remove the paperwork that blocks small exporters.
number_given: $1m pre-seed led by Ventures Platform with Voltron Capital and angels; monetisation not disclosed (likely per-document or SaaS fee plus finance spread); West Africa only, no Caribbean corridor.
source_title: Cloud9 secures $1 million to streamline cross-border trade for African SMEs
quote: Cloud9’s platform aims to automate the generation of trade documents, manage compliance requirements, and provide financing options, all within a single interface.

buyer: Diaspora individuals and small businesses holding USD/GBP/EUR and paying out locally
finding: Grey bundles multi-currency accounts with direct local-currency payout into new African corridors, targeting diaspora families rather than corporate treasury.
number_given: Funding not disclosed in this piece; monetises FX spread and transfer fees; 170+ payout destinations, all African and global corridors, no Africa-Caribbean route announced.
source_title: Nigerian fintech startup Grey launches new payout routes to Senegal, Ivory Coast, Cameroon, Rwanda
quote: With this new payout, migrants, diaspora communities, as well as individuals and businesses, can now send payments directly to recipients in these countries.

buyer: Fintechs and banks that need licensed multi-currency rails without building them
finding: Maplerad lets a business stand up a licensed payments product in minutes and settle across African borders without the correspondent banking chain that carries most of the cost.
number_given: $6m seed from Valar Ventures; API pricing not public; eight-country African footprint with no Caribbean corridor named.
source_title: Maplerad is rebuilding the rails beneath Africa’s $92bn remittance problem
quote: Rather than sending money directly to recipients, it gives businesses, banks, and fintechs the tools to move money across African borders without routing through the correspondent banking chain at all.

buyer: African SME importers and corporate treasury desks settling cross-border invoices
finding: Lumepay sells one rail-agnostic API that mixes bank rails and stablecoins so African businesses can settle cross-border invoices without stitching together several providers.
number_given: $6m pre-seed plus $10m capital float; founder-led angels and South African fintech investors; revenue model unpublished (spread/FX margin on B2B transfers); raised partly to fund a Series A.
source_title: SA fintech startup Lumepay raises $6m pre-seed round
quote: Its rail-agnostic platform combines traditional finance and stablecoins to enable fast, cost-effective and transparent B2B transfers within and across African jurisdictions.

buyer: South African online merchants and D2C brands shipping at scale
finding: Shiprazor turns 20+ courier relationships into one checkout-to-delivery integration so merchants stop juggling courier accounts and eating failed-delivery costs.
number_given: $2.65m seed led by Norrsken22 with AAIC, E4E, Tremis Capital and Google angel investors; $3.3m total raised; single-country footprint, no Caribbean activity.
source_title: SA’s Shiprazor raises $2.65m to build intelligent logistics layer for African e-commerce
quote: Through a single integration, merchants can access a network of more than 20 courier partners, optimise delivery decisions, and manage the full journey from checkout to final delivery.

finding: Four of Ghana's top five Android shopping apps at end-2025 were Chinese-owned, with Temu jumping from 5,600 to over 208,000 downloads in one quarter.
number_given: Paid acquisition and discounting; no visible Ghanaian engineering or merchant team behind the apps.
source_title: Top 5 Android Shopping Apps in Ghana: Q4 2025 Performance
quote: Temu: Shop Like a Billionaire began the quarter with a modest 5.6K downloads, which surged significantly to over 208K by the end of December.

finding: Chinese marketplaces are the main source of inbound parcels to Jamaica, reshaping local retail without any localised storefront or resident developer team.
number_given: Low-ticket direct shipping; local couriers are trying to open China-to-Jamaica routes to cut the US out of the chain.
source_title: Shipping companies say increases possible on Shein, Temu, Ali Express
quote: Chinese-made products that sell for cheap have altered the local shopping landscape in Jamaica with many small businesses purchasing in bulk for resale

finding: A Chinese founder built and then rebuilt a Nairobi fintech around real China-Africa trade flows, settling bulk container importers after an SME product flopped.
number_given: SME acquisition cost exceeded lifetime value; 90% of effort on SMEs drained cash while 10% on bulk traders sustained the team.
source_title: How a Chinese fintech founder learned to build for Kenya's reality, not its potential
quote: Long, now married to a Singaporean named George Chan and fully rooted in Kenya, co-founds Pyxis with him (with her at the helm).

finding: Chennai-based Kaleidofin set up a Kenya business and signed local bank and institutional contracts to lend into Kenya's horticulture MSMEs.
number_given: 18 months of groundwork before revenue; India-based engineering with a lean local business team.
source_title: Indian fintechs accelerate push into Global South; Kaleidofin joins ranks of Pine Labs, Razorpay
quote: Chennai-based Kaleidofin has become the latest one to foray overseas by setting up operations in Africa. The company began laying the groundwork 18 months ago and has now set up operations in Kenya.

finding: India's SUN Mobility made Nairobi and Mombasa its East Africa hub, running 35 battery-swap stations and targeting 2,500 across Africa within five years.
number_given: Sh400 daily battery plan for boda riders; capex-heavy station rollout financed with local vehicle financiers.
source_title: From petrol to battery swaps: Indian e-mobility firm makes Kenya E Africa expansion hub
quote: Kenya emerged as the company’s gateway to Africa, offering a large commercial motorcycle and three-wheeler market, supportive electric mobility policies and an established ecosystem of vehicle financiers, distributors and infrastructure partners.

buyer: Three unnamed Chinese AI firms in Nairobi's Chinatown/Kilimani
finding: Small Chinese AI firms in Nairobi modify open-weight Chinese models for Kenyan businesses, charging far less than they would earn in China.
number_given: Priced below Chinese market rates; funders absorb engineers' cost of living while credibility builds.
source_title: China's Open-Weight AI Has a Last-Mile Problem in Kenya
quote: He and his colleagues upgrade Kenyan companies’ computer systems with Chinese AI tools, for much less than they could earn in China.

finding: Jumia is onboarding thousands of Shenzhen vendors to supply Nigeria and Cote d'Ivoire, making Chinese factories the backend of African e-commerce.
number_given: Jumia takes marketplace margin as middleman; Chinese sellers ship inventory into Jumia warehouses.
source_title: How Africa's e-commerce giant is fighting off Shein and Temu
quote: We've found great potential from thousands of Chinese vendors, mostly in the Shenzhen area. We're kind of the gateway to African markets for a lot of Chinese manufacturers.

finding: Temu shipped a Nigeria-localised storefront with naira pricing and local delivery and became the country's most-downloaded app within weeks of its ad blitz.
number_given: Paid-social acquisition blitz plus subsidised nationwide delivery; Jumia's CEO says that free-delivery model is unsustainable outside major cities.
source_title: Chinese retailer Temu storms Nigeria
quote: Chinese online retailer Temu has become the most downloaded app in Nigeria on both the Android and Apple app stores in just a few weeks since ads started promoting its availability in the country.

finding: Two Chinese-owned fintechs, OPay and PalmPay, drive most of Nigeria's mobile-money growth after being preloaded on Transsion phones and pushed through agent networks.
number_given: Growth bought with free transfers then a token N10 fee, plus roughly 500,000 agents recruited on incentives.
source_title: Chinese fintechs rule as Nigeria's mobile money value jumps 29-fold
quote: OPay and PalmPay are the most prominent non-MNO-led mobile money providers and have gained significant market share in Nigeria since receiving their MMO licence

finding: Indian startups are treating Nigeria, Ghana and Kenya as their next growth market, led by edtech Leverage Edu and POS platform QueueBuster.
number_given: Asset-light entry: partnerships and remote sales, with product and engineering staying in India.
source_title: Startups eye African countries for next leg of growth
quote: We have built strong traction across Nigeria, Ghana and Kenya, recently launched in Egypt, and expect Morocco to follow soon

finding: Transsion's phone preloads give Chinese app startups instant continental distribution, letting Boomplay and PalmPay scale while African teams rarely get the same channel.
number_given: Preinstallation plus strategic investment; marginal cost of distribution near zero once the handset base exists.
source_title: How China's Technology Startups Are Scaling Across Africa
quote: With hundreds of millions of Transsion phones across the continent, they now form the basis for a massive platform that provides instant, scaled market entry for Chinese mobile technology startups trying to compete in Africa.

finding: ByteDance shipped a WeChat-style messaging app tailored to African users and shut it three years later after it failed to dislodge WhatsApp.
number_given: Three years of build and localisation spend with no monetisation path against a free incumbent.
source_title: ByteDance Shuts Down Free African Messaging App That Failed to Challenge WhatsApp
quote: Chinese tech firm ByteDance shut down its three-year-old multimedia messaging app LetsChat earlier this month, a rare defeat for the social media giant that hoped the platform would take off among Africa’s ballooning youth population.

finding: Almost every letter of credit issued by an African bank has to be confirmed by a bank outside the region before a foreign supplier or buyer will accept it - so the African side of a diaspora trade deal depends on third-party credit appetite it does not control.
number_given: Reporting on an AfDB study that also flags limited US dollar liquidity at confirming banks and counterparty concerns about African-owned banks as constraints on confirmation capacity.
source_title: ICC Digital Library - reporting on AfDB 'Trade Finance in Africa'
quote: The need for letters of credit (L/Cs) to be confirmed is a big issue since nearly all L/Cs issued by banks in Africa require confirmation when the counterparty is located outside the region.

finding: Caribbean banks have lost roughly four in ten of their correspondent banking relationships over fifteen years, cutting the region's firms off from international finance, credit and cross-border payment lines.
number_given: ~40% of correspondent banks gone over 15 years (Economist Intelligence Unit 2024 data cited); the same loss restricts cross-border payments including remittances.
source_title: Enhancing Trade Finance for SMEs in the Caribbean
quote: approximately 40% of correspondent banks have withdrawn from the Caribbean over the past 15 years, which has decreased the access of the region to international finance and credit.

finding: Credit and political risk insurance cover for Africa is sold out: demand far exceeds capacity and insurer country limits are already full, which leaves deals unfinanceable rather than merely expensive.
number_given: Guillaume Simonnet, senior director, Willis Credit Risk Solutions, on the record: demand for credit and political risk insurance far outstrips available capacity, particularly in Africa.
source_title: Unlocking infrastructure finance with first-loss guarantee structures
quote: There is too much to do and insufficient money and capacity in Sub-Saharan Africa.

finding: Double-tax relief cannot be planned around: treaties get signed and then sit unratified, so withholding tax and double taxation fall on firms that assumed a treaty applied. Nigeria - a primary diaspora investment destination - has no income tax treaty in force with the United States.
number_given: Non-treaty withholding on dividends, interest and royalties to non-residents is 10% in Nigeria; no US treaty appears in the in-force treaty table, so US investors get no reduced rate.
source_title: Nigeria - Corporate - Withholding taxes (Worldwide Tax Summaries)
quote: Nigeria also has tax treaties with Kenya, Mauritius, and Poland; however, these treaties have not been ratified by the Nigerian National Assembly.

finding: Moving capital into African and Caribbean markets through bank rails costs roughly triple the G20 efficiency target, and banks are the most expensive channel of all - so every dollar a diaspora firm sends to fund an African or Caribbean operation, supplier or subsidiary loses value before it lands.
number_given: 13.40% average total cost via banks vs 3% G20 target; Sub-Saharan Africa is the most expensive receiving region at 8.37% average across all provider types.
source_title: Remittance Prices Worldwide - Issue 50, June 2024
quote: Banks remain the most expensive type of service provider, with an average cost of 13.40 percent.

finding: Profits earned in an African market can be legally repatriable and still not leave: companies have had dividends suspended and revenues trapped for lack of foreign exchange.
number_given: $280m of MTN earnings stuck in 2020 forcing a dividend suspension; $464m of foreign airline ticket revenue blocked by July 2022; a ~$7bn FX backlog was later cleared.
source_title: Multinationals repatriate $2.8bn in five years despite FX squeeze
quote: In 2020, MTN Group, a major telecommunications operator, encountered difficulties repatriating approximately $280 million in earnings from Nigeria.

finding: Sanctions screening volume has outrun the compliance capacity of the institutions diaspora firms bank with, so onboarding a new African or Caribbean counterparty means queuing behind an alert backlog.
number_given: Total financial crime compliance cost in the US and Canada reached US$61 billion; 99% of institutions reported cost increases; 79% saw KYC/compliance technology costs rise.
source_title: True Cost of Financial Crime Compliance Study - U.S. and Canada
quote: At 83% of mid and large-sized organizations and 87% of small organizations (holding less than $10 billion in assets), the number of screening alerts has increased.

finding: The Black-owned exporter base in the US is tiny and shrinking - about 1,100 firms - so there is no existing cohort of Black firms with the export infrastructure to step into African and Caribbean trade.
number_given: Of 160,697 US employer firms that exported, only 1,139 were Black-owned and 15,903 Asian-owned; 16% of exporting firms are owned by people of color.
source_title: How to Triple the Number of Minority Exporters
quote: From 2019 to 2020, Black-owned employer firms that export declined by 34%.

finding: The US government platform that was brokering and de-risking Africa deals for diaspora firms - the USAID Africa Trade and Investment activity under Prosper Africa - was terminated mid-programme, removing deal sourcing, market intelligence and transaction advisory that firms had come to rely on.
number_given: Before termination the activity had closed 3,481 trade deals worth $2 billion and 483 investment deals worth $1.2 billion across 50 countries - capacity that is now gone.
source_title: Africa-USAID Africa Trade and Investment activity
quote: This project was terminated ahead of schedule following the Secretary of State's review of U.S. foreign assistance in 2025.

finding: The barriers to Africa-Caribbean commerce are named and structural - inadequate transport and connectivity, scarce trade and project finance, and misaligned regulation - not a lack of commercial interest.
number_given: ACTIF2025 announced over US$300 million of deals across infrastructure, manufacturing, logistics, digital services, tourism and agribusiness; the forum also urged the remaining CARICOM states to sign Afreximbank's partnership agreement (13 had signed).
source_title: Fourth AfriCaribbean Trade and Investment Forum Communique
quote: including inadequate transportation and connectivity, limited access to trade and project finance, and regulatory misalignment

finding: The diaspora has a seat allocated at the African Union and no machinery to use it: 20 diaspora seats sat empty for two decades because no legal framework existed, so diaspora business bodies had no formal route into AU policy or procurement.
number_given: The Diaspora Legal Framework was only endorsed in 2025; election of the 20 diaspora representatives had not yet occurred, so the channel is still being stood up.
source_title: The African Diaspora's Seat at the Table: Understanding ECOSOCC's Diaspora Legal Framework
quote: Yet, despite the allocation of 20 seats for diaspora CSOs in ECOSOCC's General Assembly, the lack of an institutional framework prevented their inclusion for over 20 years.

finding: There is effectively no Africa-Caribbean trade lane to plug into: African goods exports to the Caribbean are a rounding error and Caribbean exports to Africa are under one percent, so a diaspora firm cannot simply extend an existing supply chain across the Atlantic.
number_given: Trade in both directions is concentrated in a handful of sectors; ITC and Afreximbank estimate trade could rise by up to $1.8 billion by 2028 if tariff and non-tariff barriers are addressed.
source_title: Connecting regions and diasporas through trade: Towards deeper African-Caribbean ties
quote: Only 0.1% of African goods exports are destined for the Caribbean, and Caribbean goods exports to Africa remain below 1% of the region's total.

finding: Trade preference that diaspora-linked supply chains were built on is authorized in short increments, so investors cannot underwrite a factory or offtake deal against it.
number_given: AGOA lapsed 30 September 2025 and was retroactively reauthorized only through 31 December 2026; UNCTAD puts the tariff cost of the lapse at $560 million based on 2023 import values.
source_title: African Growth and Opportunity Act (AGOA) - CRS Report R49187
quote: Historically, many AGOA-linked investors have called for longer, more predictable authorization periods.

finding: West African banks reject trade finance applications largely because borrowers cannot post collateral and are judged high-risk - the two things a growing diaspora-owned firm is least able to fix.
number_given: 45-67% of surveyed banks cite collateral gaps and applicant risk as the leading rejection reasons; the same report notes firms self-exclude from trade after prior rejections.
source_title: Trade Finance in West Africa
quote: Between 45 percent and 67 percent of banks across the four countries mention lack of collateral and high applicant risk as the top causes of rejection.

buyer: Prime Minister Gaston Browne, CARICOM Chair
finding: The CARICOM chair opened the first Africa-CARICOM summit by stating there had never been trade between the two regions at all.
number_given: No figures; the summit proposed a joint market of ~1.4bn people and 69 UN votes.
source_title: Create pathways of accord between Africa, the Caribbean - CARICOM Chair at historic #AfricaCARICOMSummit
quote: Let us be clear: There was never trade between Africa and the Caribbean.

finding: The forum's US$300m of deals were all Caribbean borrowers; not one had an East African counterparty.
number_given: US$300m+ across eight deals; US$4bn+ across three years of ACTIF.
source_title: ACTIF 2025 closes with over USD 300 million in deals and bold commitments to integration, mobility and investment
quote: A total of eight major deals and memoranda were announced over the course of the forum, spanning infrastructure, tourism, digital transformation, and trade finance

finding: The flagship Africa-Caribbean forum was still only promising to create direct air and sea links in 2025, four years after a bilateral air services treaty was signed.
number_given: No costed figure for the air or maritime links; the forum separately announced US$300m in deals, all Caribbean-side.
source_title: Fourth AfriCaribbean Trade and Investment Forum Communique and Final Remarks
publisher: African Export-Import Bank (Afreximbank) and Government of Grenada
quote: support, and fast-track the implementation of enabling policies and instruments to establish direct air and maritime links between Africa and the Caribbean

buyer: EAC Secretariat / Deputy Secretary-General Annette Mutaawe Ssemuwemba
finding: The EAC's own trade data shows its export gravity is Asia and intra-Africa, with the Caribbean not registering at all.
number_given: 28% of EAC exports intra-African; 56% to Asia; intra-African trade is 16% of Africa's total.
source_title: EAC boosts Intra-African Trade as continental integration gains momentum
quote: the majority of EAC’s trade remained externally oriented, with Asia accounting for 56% of exports and 64% of imports

finding: An Air Services Agreement and a joint trade committee were signed in 2021 and produced no measurable trade or connectivity.
number_given: No figures disclosed.
source_title: Barbados & Kenya Sign Three Agreements
quote: They are an Air Services Agreement, a Memorandum of Understanding in the Establishment of a Joint Committee on Trade Investment, and a Memorandum of Understanding in the Development of the National Botanical Garden.

buyer: Ministry of Foreign and Diaspora Affairs, Kenya
finding: Kenya is betting a resident High Commission in Kingston can turn a near-zero Jamaica trade relationship into access to the whole CARICOM market.
number_given: No figures given; mission is a relocation of the Havana embassy, so incremental cost is low.
source_title: Kenya Opens Resident High Commission in Jamaica, Expands Diplomatic Presence in the Caribbean
publisher: Ministry of Foreign and Diaspora Affairs, Republic of Kenya
quote: Jamaica serves as an important gateway to the wider CARICOM market, presenting new opportunities for Kenyan businesses to expand trade and investment across the Caribbean.

finding: Kenya's president publicly committed to direct East Africa-Caribbean flights in 2019 and no such route exists seven years later.
number_given: Kenya Airways had just opened Nairobi-New York; the Caribbean route would have been an additional long-haul on a loss-making carrier.
source_title: Kenya and Jamaica pledge to deepen trade ties
publisher: Nation Media Group (Daily Nation), quoting President Kenyatta on the record
quote: we would like to see flights flying from the East Coast to the West Coast of Africa and directly to Jamaica, and through Jamaica to the rest of the Caribbean

finding: Rwanda's president told Jamaica's parliament in 2022 that Kigali wanted closer trade and investment cooperation, and no material trade followed.
number_given: No figures given.
source_title: Joint Sitting of the Houses of Parliament of Jamaica - Address by President Kagame
publisher: Office of the President of Rwanda (official transcript)
quote: As Rwanda, we are also keen to cooperate with Jamaica much more closely and share experiences in trade and investment, as well as national unity and citizen development.

finding: Tanzania sent its Prime Minister to the Caribbean forum but asked for better investment conditions rather than announcing any East African deal.
number_given: Forum-wide: over US$4bn in agreements signed across three years of ACTIF; Tanzania announced none of it.
source_title: PM urges ACTIF to deliver solutions
quote: He also stressed the need for both African and Caribbean nations to create conducive environments for attracting investment and to demonstrate strong cooperation with investors who are ready to commit to long-term ventures in the region.

finding: Uganda's diaspora outreach is aimed at inbound American capital and tourism, not at two-way trade with the Caribbean.
number_given: No figures; the delegation discussed manufacturing, tourism, coffee, banana flour, vanilla and a computer assembly plant.
source_title: President Museveni Calls On Investors To Take Advantage Of Uganda's Economic Potential
publisher: State House Uganda (Office of the President)
quote: I am very happy to meet you. You are most welcome here in Uganda. This is the right place and time to invest. We have everything here.

buyer: National Procurement and Tender Administration Board (NPTAB), Ministry of Finance
finding: Guyana is spending GYD 145.2m this year to replace paper tendering with an end-to-end e-tender lifecycle, a digital bidders register and an e-marketplace, creating a single state buyer for procurement software and integration work.
number_given: GYD 145.2m allocated in the 2026 budget; 25-30% of procurement to be set aside for SMEs; newpaper tender advertising said to cost the state close to GYD 800m a year.
source_title: Government to roll out fully digital procurement system by year-end
quote: The e-tender lifecycle module will digitise the full tender process end-to-end, from procurement planning and tender creation through bid submission, evaluation, contract award, administration, variation and payment processing

finding: A five-person Jamaican AI support startup already runs four government pilots and is converting a JAMPRO Guyana mission into pilots, so Caribbean buyers meet a dialect-trained local vendor before any outside agency.
number_given: Won J$4M patent grant from the Development Bank of Jamaica; targets banks, government agencies; expanding to Guyana then sub-Saharan Africa.
source_title: Chatflow Harnesses AI To Revolutionise Customer Service
quote: My goal now is to complete some pilots with some of those businesses and to ensure that, after due diligence and we've onboarded them, that we can serve their consumers better
